title: Chapter 6 — Judicial Power In The United States
paragraphs: Judicial Power in the United States and Its Influence on Political Society.

I have thought it essential to devote a separate chapter to the judicial authorities of the United States, so that their great political importance will not be diminished in the reader’s eyes by a merely incidental mention. Confederations have existed in countries other than America, and republics have been set up on more than just the shores of the New World. The representative system has been adopted in several European States, but I am not aware of any nation on earth that has organized a judicial power on the principle the Americans have now adopted. The judicial organization of the United States is the institution a foreigner finds hardest to understand. He hears the authority of a judge invoked in the political events of every day, and he naturally concludes that in the United States the judges are important political officials. Yet when he examines the nature of the courts, they offer nothing contrary to the usual habits and privileges of such bodies, and the magistrates seem to him to intervene in public affairs by chance — but by a chance that recurs daily.

When the Parliament of Paris protested, refused to register an edict, or summoned an official accused of corruption to its bar, its political influence as a judicial body was clearly visible. Nothing of the kind is to be seen in the United States. The Americans have kept all the ordinary characteristics of judicial authority and have carefully restricted its action to the ordinary range of its functions.

The first characteristic of judicial power in all nations is the duty of arbitration. But rights must be contested for a court to intervene, and an action must be brought before a judge can rule. So long as the law is uncontested, the judicial authority is not called on to discuss it, and it may exist without being noticed. When a judge, in a particular case, challenges a law bearing on that case, he expands the circle of his ordinary duties without stepping outside it, since he is in some measure obliged to rule on the law in order to rule on the case. But if he pronounces on a law without resting on a case, he plainly steps beyond his own sphere and invades that of the legislature.

The second characteristic of judicial power is that it rules on particular cases, not on general principles. If a judge, in deciding a specific point, destroys a general principle by issuing a judgment that tends to reject all the inferences from that principle — and thus annul it — he still remains within the ordinary limits of his office. But if he directly attacks a general principle without having a particular case in view, he steps outside the circle in which all nations have agreed to confine his authority. He takes on a more important, and perhaps more useful, role than that of a magistrate, but he ceases to be a representative of the judicial power.

The third characteristic of the judicial power is that it cannot act unless it is appealed to, or until a matter has been brought before it. This characteristic is less universal than the other two, but despite the exceptions, I think it can be regarded as essential. The judicial power is by its nature inert; it must be set in motion to produce a result. When it is called on to repress a crime, it punishes the criminal; when a wrong must be redressed, it is ready to redress it; when an act requires interpretation, it is prepared to interpret it. But it does not pursue criminals, hunt out wrongs, or examine evidence on its own initiative. A judicial officer who opened proceedings on his own and usurped the role of censor of the laws would in some measure do violence to the passive nature of his authority.

The Americans have kept these three distinguishing characteristics of judicial power. An American judge can only render a decision when litigation has arisen; he deals only with particular cases; and he cannot act until the case has been duly brought before the court. His position is therefore exactly like that of the magistrate in other nations — and yet he is vested with immense political power. If the scope of his authority and his means of action are the same as those of other judges, one must ask where he derives a power they do not possess. The cause of this difference lies in a simple fact: the Americans have recognized the right of judges to base their decisions on the constitution rather than on statutes. In other words, they have left judges free not to apply laws that appear to them to be unconstitutional.

I am aware that a similar right has been claimed — but claimed in vain — by courts in other countries. In America, however, it is recognized by all authorities, and not a party, not even an individual, is found to contest it. This fact can only be explained by the principles of the American constitution. In France the constitution is (or at least is presumed to be) immutable, and the received doctrine is that no power has the right to change any part of it. In England, Parliament has an acknowledged right to modify the constitution; since the constitution can therefore undergo continual change, it does not in reality exist. Parliament is at once a legislative and a constituent assembly. The political theories of America are simpler and more rational. An American constitution is not assumed to be immutable as in France, nor is it open to modification by the ordinary powers of society as in England. It forms a distinct whole which, as it represents the determination of the whole people, is no less binding on the legislator than on the private citizen; but it may be altered by the will of the people, in predetermined cases, according to established rules. In America the constitution may therefore change, but as long as it exists it is the source of all authority and the sole vehicle of the dominant force. *a

a [ [The fifth article of the original Constitution of the United States provides the mode in which amendments of the Constitution may be made. Amendments must be proposed by two-thirds of both Houses of Congress, and ratified by the Legislatures of three-fourths of the several States. Fifteen amendments of the Constitution have been made at different times since 1789, the most important of which are the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth, framed and ratified after the Civil War. The original Constitution of the United States, followed by these fifteen amendments, is printed at the end of this edition. —Translator’s Note, 1874.]]

It is easy to see how these differences must affect the position and rights of the judicial bodies in the three countries I have cited. If the courts in France were authorized to disobey laws on the grounds that they conflicted with the constitution, the supreme power would effectively fall into their hands, since they alone would have the right to interpret a constitution whose clauses no authority can modify. They would therefore take the place of the nation and exercise as absolute a sway over society as the inherent weakness of judicial power would allow. It is true that, since French judges are not competent to declare a law unconstitutional, the power of changing the constitution is indirectly granted to the legislature, because no legal barrier would obstruct the alterations it might prescribe. But it is better to grant the power of changing the people’s constitution to men who represent (however imperfectly) the will of the people than to men who represent no one but themselves.

It would be still more unreasonable to give English judges the right to resist the decisions of the legislature, since the Parliament that makes the laws also makes the constitution. Consequently, a law that emanates from the three powers of the State can in no case be unconstitutional. But neither of these observations applies to America.

In the United States the constitution governs the legislator as much as the private citizen. Since it is the first of laws, it cannot be modified by an ordinary law, and it is therefore right that the courts should obey the constitution in preference to any statute. This condition is essential to the power of the judiciary, for it is every magistrate’s natural right to choose the legal obligation that most strictly binds him.

In France the constitution is also the first of laws, and judges have the same right to base their decisions on it. But if they were to exercise that right, they would necessarily encroach on rights more sacred than their own — those of society, in whose name they act. In that case the interest of the State clearly prevails over the motives of an individual. In America, where the nation can always bring its magistrates back into line by changing its constitution, no such danger is to be feared. On this point, then, the political and the logical reasons agree, and the people and the judges alike retain their privileges.

Whenever a law the judge considers unconstitutional is argued before a court in the United States, he may refuse to accept it as a rule. This power is the only one unique to the American magistrate, but it gives rise to immense political influence. Few laws can escape the searching analysis of the judicial power for long, because few are not prejudicial to some private interest, and none cannot be brought before a court by the choice of the parties or by the necessity of the case. But from the moment a judge has refused to apply a given law in a case, that law loses part of its moral force. Those whose interests it harms learn that there are ways to evade its authority; similar suits multiply, until it becomes powerless. At that point one of two alternatives must be chosen: the people must change the constitution, or the legislature must repeal the law. The political power the Americans have entrusted to their courts is therefore immense, but its dangers are considerably reduced by the obligation to attack laws only through the courts. If the judge had been empowered to contest laws on grounds of theoretical generalities — if he could open an attack on the legislator or issue a censure — he would have played a prominent part in the political arena. As the champion or adversary of a party, he would have marshaled the hostile passions of the nation into the conflict. But when a judge contests a law applied to a particular case, in an obscure proceeding, the importance of his attack is hidden from public view. His decision bears on an individual’s interest, and if the law is slighted, it is only incidentally. What is more, though the law is censured, it is not abolished; its moral force may be weakened, but its force as law is not suspended. Its final destruction can only be achieved by the repeated attacks of judicial officers. It is easy to see how, by linking the censorship of laws to the private interests of citizens and by intimately joining the prosecution of the law to the prosecution of an individual, legislation is protected from reckless attackers and from the daily aggressions of party spirit. The legislator’s errors are exposed at the very moments when their bad consequences are most felt, and it is always a concrete, demonstrable fact that serves as the basis of the prosecution.

I am inclined to believe that this practice of the American courts is at once the most favorable to liberty and to public order. If the judge could only attack the legislator openly and directly, he would sometimes be afraid to offer any resistance to his will, while at other moments party spirit might encourage him to defy it at every turn. The laws would then be attacked when the power they came from was weak, and obeyed when it was strong. In other words, they would be contested when it would be useful to respect them, and respected when they would be easy to turn into instruments of oppression. The American judge, however, is brought into the political arena independently of his own will. He rules on the law only because he is obliged to rule on a case. The political question he is called on to resolve is tied to the interests of the litigants, and he cannot refuse to decide it without abdicating the duties of his office. He performs his public role as a citizen by fulfilling the precise duties of his profession as a magistrate. It is true that under this system the judicial censorship exercised by the courts over legislation cannot extend to all laws indiscriminately, since some of them can never give rise to the specific kind of dispute called a lawsuit. And even when such a dispute is possible, it may happen that no one cares to bring it before a court. The Americans have often felt this disadvantage, but they have left the remedy incomplete, for fear of giving it an efficacy that might in some cases prove dangerous. Within these limits, the power vested in the American courts to declare a statute unconstitutional is one of the most powerful barriers ever devised against the tyranny of political assemblies.
Other Powers Granted to American Judges

In the United States all citizens have the right to indict public officials before the ordinary courts — How they use this right — Article 75 of the French Constitution of the Year VIII — The Americans and the English cannot understand the purport of this clause.

It is perfectly natural that in a free country like America, all citizens should have the right to indict public officials before the ordinary courts, and that all judges should have the power to punish public offenses. The right granted to the courts to try the agents of the executive when they have broken the laws is so natural that it cannot be considered an extraordinary privilege. Nor does it seem to me that the springs of government are weakened in the United States by the custom of making all public officers answerable to the judges of the land. On the contrary, the Americans seem to me to have increased by this means the respect due to the authorities, and at the same time to have made those in power more careful about offending public opinion. I was struck by the small number of political trials that take place in the United States, but I had no difficulty accounting for it. A lawsuit, of whatever kind, is always a difficult and expensive undertaking. It is easy to attack a public man in a newspaper, but the grounds required to warrant a legal action must be serious. A solid basis for complaint is therefore needed to induce someone to prosecute a public officer, and public officers are careful not to provide such grounds when they fear being prosecuted.

This does not depend on the republican form of American institutions, for the same facts appear in England. These two nations do not regard the impeachment of the chief officers of State as a sufficient guarantee of their independence. They hold that the right of minor prosecutions, within reach of the whole community, is a better pledge of freedom than those great judicial actions which are rarely employed until it is too late.

In the Middle Ages, when it was very hard to catch offenders, the judges inflicted the most dreadful tortures on the few who were arrested — which did nothing to reduce the number of crimes. It has since been discovered that when justice is more certain and more mild, it is at the same time more effective. The English and the Americans hold that tyranny and oppression should be treated like any other crime: by reducing the penalty and making conviction easier.

In the Year VIII of the French Republic a constitution was drawn up in which the following clause was introduced: “Art. 75. All the agents of the government below the rank of ministers can only be prosecuted for offences relating to their several functions by virtue of a decree of the Conseil d’Etat; in which case the prosecution takes place before the ordinary tribunals.” This clause survived the “Constitution de l’An VIII” and is still maintained, in spite of the just complaints of the nation. I have always found the greatest difficulty in explaining its meaning to Englishmen or Americans. They were immediately led to conclude that the Conseil d’Etat in France was a great court, set up at the center of the kingdom, which exercised a preliminary and somewhat tyrannical jurisdiction over all political cases. But when I told them that the Conseil d’Etat was not a judicial body in the ordinary sense, but an administrative council made up of men dependent on the Crown — so that the king, after ordering one of his servants (called a Prefect) to commit an injustice, has the power to order another of his servants (called a Councillor of State) to prevent the first from being punished; when I demonstrated to them that the citizen injured by the sovereign’s order is obliged to ask the sovereign for permission to seek redress — they refused to believe so flagrant an abuse, and were tempted to accuse me of falsehood or ignorance. It often happened before the Revolution that a Parliament issued a warrant against a public officer who had committed an offense, and sometimes the proceedings were stopped by the authority of the Crown, which enforced compliance with its absolute and despotic will. It is painful to see how much lower we have sunk than our forefathers, since we now let things pass under the color of justice and the sanction of the law that once only violence could impose.
